references.text: The Lord predicts that He will harden Pharaoh's heart, so that he will not let the people go. This is the first mention of God hardening Pharaoh.
Pharaoh's heart was hardened, and he did not listen to Moses and Aaron, just as the Lord had said. The same pattern as in 10:20.
Pharaoh's heart remained stubborn, and he did not listen to them, just as the Lord had said. A repeated theme of a hardened heart.
Pharaoh hardened his own heart and did not listen to them. Shows the continuing pattern of hardening.
Pharaoh hardened his heart again this time and would not let the people go. Parallel wording with refusing to release the children of Israel.
The Lord hardened Pharaoh's heart, and he did not listen to them, just as the Lord had said to Moses. A direct parallel where the Lord actively hardens.
Pharaoh's heart was hardened, and he would not let the children of Israel go. The same wording with חזק and refusing to release the children of Israel.
The Lord hardened Pharaoh's heart, and he was unwilling to let them go. Almost identical verse appearing later in the same chapter.
The Lord hardened Pharaoh's heart, so that he would not let the children of Israel leave his land. A summary of the hardening theme before the final plague.
The Lord hardened Pharaoh's heart, so he pursued the Israelites. Shows that the hardening continued even after the exodus from Egypt.
Paul quotes the story of Pharaoh as an example of God's sovereign will to harden whom He wills. A theological reflection on Pharaoh's hardening.
Reveals the theological dynamic between human self-hardening and God's active hardening.
Shows that Pharaoh's refusal is a fulfillment of God's prophecy about a hardened heart.
Illustrates that Pharaoh's stubborn mind persists even when the plagues cause no immediate harm.
Reveals Pharaoh's active role in hardening his own heart in response to God's intervention.
